Preeclampsia (PE), a severe hypertensive disorder during pregnancy, signiﬁcantly contributes to maternal and neonatal mortality. Existing prediction biomarkers are often invasive and expensive, hindering their widespread application. This study introduces PROMPT (Preeclampsia Risk factor + Ophthalmic data + Mean arterial pressure Prediction Test), an AI-driven model leveraging retinal photography for PE prediction, registered at ChiCTR (ChiCTR2100049850) in August 2021. Analyzing 1812 pregnancies before 14 gestational weeks, we extracted retinal parameters using a deep learning system. The PROMPT achieved an AUC of 0.87 (0.83–0.90) for PE prediction and 0.91 (0.85–0.97) for preterm PE prediction using machine learning, signiﬁcantly outperforming the baseline model (p < 0.001). It also improved detection of severe adverse pregnancy outcomes from 35% to 41%. Economically, PROMPT was estimated to avert 1809 PE cases and saved over $50 million per 100,000 screenings. These results position PROMPT as a non-invasive and cost-effective tool for prenatal care, especially valuable in low- and middle-income countries.

Preeclampsia (PE) is a life-threatening hypertensive disorder in pregnancy and a major cause of maternal and neonatal morbidity and mortality, which affects around 4.6% of pregnant women worldwide1. It results in an increased riskof adversepregnancyoutcomes(AO) including pretermbirth (PTB), small for gestational age (SGA), and even stillbirth, ranking the second leading cause of maternal mortality in China2. Such outcomes highlight the need for accessible tools for identifying high-risk pregnancies before clinical presentation, especially in low-and-middle-income countries (LMICs)3,4. Assessment for pregnant women at high-risk for PE based on risk factors of maternal characteristics and obstetric history, such as advanced maternal age, chronic hypertension, renal disease, obesity, and PE history, has shown suboptimal performance and cannot

quantify patient-speciﬁc risk5–7. Recent research has advanced the identiﬁcation of novel biomarkers to predict PE in early pregnancy. The Fetal Medicine Foundation triple test, which combines maternal risk factors with biomarkers including mean arterial pressure (MAP), uterine artery pulsatility index (UtA-PI), placental growth factor (PlGF) and pregnancy-associated plasma protein-A (PAPP-A), has achieved moderate to high discrimination in different populations7–11. However, the need for a qualiﬁed sonographer to measure UtA-PI and additional blood sampling for serum markers limits their widespread application in clinical practice, especially in resource-limited areas. Analysis of circulating cell-free DNA (cfDNA) methylation and cellfree RNA also offers the possibility of early prediction of PE but is expensive and beyond the reach of clinical practice12–14. Mounting evidence has shown that the eye can serve as a ‘window’, i.e., the sentinel sensory organ, to observe microvascular alterations in systemic disorders15–19. In obstetric clinical practice, the PE patients are referred to retinal examinations in case of ophthalmic complications. However, whether ocular manifestations occur before PE diagnosis has not been fully explored. We performed a prospective cohort to observe the early retinal featuresbeforePEoccurrenceand foundthatvascularchangesweremarked in early pregnancy before the onset of symptoms and clinical diagnosis. In this study, we present a machine-learning (ML) based algorithm for PE prediction using retinal vascular features in a non-invasive and costeffective approach. The DR rose to 16.5%, 22.4%, and 23.4% at FPR of 10%, and 23.9%, 28.2%, and 31.0% at FPR of 15%. For severe AO, the three models could achieve DR of 13.3%, 22.4%, and 27.6% at FPR of 5%, and 21.4%, 31.6%, and 35.7% at FPR of 10%. When it comes to FPR of 15%, the DR were 34.7%, 37.8%, and 40.8%, respectively, indicating a higher DR of AO and severe AO using the PROMPT model compared with the baseline and MAP models.

Economic evaluation of different PE prediction models The total costs per person for no prediction, the baseline, MAP, and PROMPT prediction models were $2142.63, $2104.60, $2096.52, and $2091.29, respectively (Table 4). The PROMPT model was proved dominant to the other prediction methods, averting more PE cases while saving total societal costs. The PROMPT model could avoid 1809, 416, and 380 cases of PE per 100,000 pregnancy women screened in the frist trimester compared with no prediction, the baseline, and MAP prediction. An extensive sensitivity analysis was conducted to prove that the base-case results were robust to a broad range of parameter values. The one-way and probability sensitivity analysis showed the PROMPT model was costeffective to other strategies, which were robust to randomly distributed parameters (Supplementary Fig. 3). The cost-effectiveness acceptability curve diagrams showed that PROMPT model was the best strategy, accounting for 96.3% of the simulations in total situations (Supplementary Fig. 4).

Discussion This work provides evidence that the retinal vascular features are potential biomarkers for PE prediction and AO detection. These retinal biomarkers have several desirable properties. Compared with recent biomarkers reported, retinal photography is non-invasive, convenient, and accessible, especially in rural areas where quality resources are lacking. Besides, the PROMPT model is proved dominant in the cost-effective analysis, averting more PE cases while saving total societal costs, which presents an opportunity to promote equity of pregnancy health in LMICs from the societal perspective. In this study, the metadata variables (MAP, overweight, renal disease history, and PE history), and the retinal parameters (AVR, tortD, etc.) included in the model were consistent with literature and clinical experience6,27. In the routine clinical practice, patients diagnosed with PE were referred to retinal examinations for complications like retinal hemorrhage, exudation, and detachment. However, the status quo focuses on ophthalmic manifestations after PE diagnosis and the quantiﬁcation parameters are lacking. There was limited study on early ophthalmic characteristics prior to PE incidence and related pregnancy outcomes. Taking the advantage of deep learning algorithm, fully automate retinal microvasculature segmentation and quantiﬁcation were achieved and we were able to utilize numeric retinal parameters for PErisk assessment29. Our study demonstrated that the retinal vascular alterations were found in the ﬁrst trimester of pregnancy, much prior to the PE diagnosis, indicating the potential to be early and sensitive biomarkers. In the PROMPT model, ﬁve retinal vascular parameters (AVR, VSD, tortD, angtort, and angtort_std) were selectedas variables by LASSO. Our study has the following strengths. We prospectively collected ocular data in the ﬁrst trimester of pregnancy, allowing us to observe the associations between retinal alterations before the onset of PE. In this study, we focused on parameters collected from 11-13+6 weeks of gestation, as this representstheearliestfeasibletimeframetoassesspregnantwomen’sriskfor PE. This time window aligns with the timing of most pregnancies’ ﬁrst prenatal visits and is consistent with both domestic guidelines and international screening strategies27,45. Early ﬁrst-trimester screening also allows for timely prophylactic interventions, such as blood pressure monitoring and aspirin prescription. Then, we utilized DL-based system for retinal vessel segmentation and qualiﬁcation, thus extracting the early and subtle vascular features before PE. Next, we employed ML algorithms to construct a model with good performance of PE and preterm PE prediction, in which only three types of data and nine variables were selected, making it easy to apply in clinical practice. Hence, it provides a non-invasive, accessible, and cost-effective way for prenatal care. Our study is subject to certain limitations, notably the need to increase both the sample size and data diversity. Due to low prevenance of PE, prospective cohort construction, and followup periods for pregnancy outcomes, the data acquisition faces a series of challenges. Considering the relatively small number of PE cases, we employed 10-fold CV to test the robustness of the model instead of a separate test set. Future study in other centers is needed to verify the robustness of the PROMPT model. Finally, our work shows that advances in AI can provide new clinical insights by addressing important unsolved challenges and allowing for the development of new biomarkers. By quantifying the early retinal vascular characteristics using DL-based system, this study provides initial evidence of the retinal vascular biomarkers to improve PE prediction and AO detection. The PROMPT model, including four clinical variables and ﬁve ophthalmic parameters from one single retinal photograph, is a non-invasive, cost-effective, and convenient method for pregnancy health management in low-resource settings. The large-scale real-world evaluation of PROMPT model warrants further investigation before clinical implementation.

Methods Study design and participants This was a prospective cohort study conducted at the Department of Obstetrics in the First Afﬁliated Hospital (FAH), Sun Yat-sen University from August 2021 to November 2023. The inclusion criteria for the study were as follows: age ≥18 years old, singleton pregnancy and 11-13+6 weeks of gestation at the booking visit. The exclusion criteria were a history of ocular surgery history, cataract, severe opacity of refractive media, severe systemic illness, or signiﬁcant mental illness or those for whom a major fetal abnormality was identiﬁed at the time of recruitment. Introduction Fetal growth restriction (FGR) is a significant perinatal complication that occurs when a fetus fails to achieve its biological growth potential [1]. The etiology of FGR is multifactorial, encompassing maternal characteristics, fetal conditions, placental dysfunction (including epigen­ etic dysregulation) [2], and umbilical cord abnormalities. FGR increases the incidence of preterm birth, fetal dis­ tress, and neonatal asphyxia [3], contributing to higher perinatal morbidity and mortality [4]. Early diagnosis and timely intervention are critical for improving outcomes for infants with FGR [5].

Traditional clinical methods, such as maternal risk fac­ tors, fetal biometry, and Doppler ultrasound, have been used to predict FGR [6]. However, the accuracy of these approaches remains suboptimal. Advances in molecular biology and genomics have led to growing interest in cellfree RNA (cfRNA) as a potential non-invasive biomarker. During pregnancy, cfRNA consists of small RNA mole­ cules that circulate in maternal blood and may originate from placental, fetal, or maternal tissues. This real-time biomarker offers a promising method to monitor preg­ nancy pathophysiology and detect specific physiological changes.

Recent studies have demonstrated that cfRNA can esti­ mate gestational age and predict risks for conditions such as preeclampsia [7] and preterm delivery [8]. However, its role in predicting FGR remains underexplored. There­ fore, the aim of this study was to investigate the poten­ tial of cfRNA as a non-invasive and early biomarker to improve the accuracy of FGR prediction. By leveraging machine learning approaches, we seek to comprehen­ sively evaluate the feasibility and clinical utility of cfRNA for enhancing FGR prediction and guiding management strategies.

Materials and methods Study design and population This case-control study explored the potential of using cfRNA in maternal plasma as a biomarker for identify­ ing FGR. The singleton pregnant women from January 2021 to January 2022 in the First Affiliated Hospital of Sun Yat-sen University with non-invasive prenatal test (NIPT) data. The remaining plasma samples after NIPT detection were stored in -80℃ with the approval of participants.

The inclusion criteria for this study were a diagnosis of FGR and the availability of stored plasma samples fol­ lowing NIPT at our hospital. FGR was diagnosed when ultrasound estimated fetal weight or abdominal circum­ ference was below the 10th percentile for the correspond­ ing gestational age, according to the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) guidelines [3]. The exclusion criteria were as follows: the gestational age for blood extraction >28 weeks, aneuploidy and fetal structural abnormalities, fetal anomaly, preeclamp­ sia, gestational diabetes mellitus, autoimmune disease and multiple pregnancy. The control group consisted of pregnancies without any complications. Each FGR sample was matched with approximately four controls according to maternal age and body mass index (BMI) before gestation. The sample size was determined prag­ matically based on available eligible samples during the study period, including all consecutively identified FGR cases meeting the criteria (n = 39) and approximately four matched controls per case (n = 133).

To explore FGR from a longitudinal developmental perspective, the microarray dataset of FGR placentas (GSE100415) was downloaded from the Gene Expression Omnibus database. Following data cleaning, 49 FGR sam­ ples and 26 control samples were included in the analysis.

Analysis of CfRNA and placenta data Plasma samples were stored at -80  °C for further pro­ cessing. The extraction of circulating nucleic acid was performed using a column-based extraction kit, follow­ ing the instructions provided by the manufacturer (RNA extraction kit, VISION MEDICALS, Guangzhou, China). After extraction, the nucleic acid concentration was mea­ sured by Qubit 4.0 fluorometer (Invitrogen, Carlsbad, CA, USA). RNA purification, one-strand and secondstrand synthesis, and RNA-sequencing library construc­ tion were performed using the RNA library building kit (VISION MEDICALS, Guangzhou, China) according to the manufacturer’s protocol. The library concentration was detected by Qubit 4.0 fluorometer (Invitrogen, Carls­ bad, CA, USA). At last, the libraries were pooled and sequenced on the NextSeqCN500 sequencing platform (Illumina, San Diego, CA, USA).

Machine learning The least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) is a statistical regression technique used for fea­ ture selection and regularization. In this study, LASSO logistic algorithm was used to further select the most predictive genes for FGR prediction by the “glmnet” [13] and “cv.glmnet” R packages. We selected lambda(λ) based on the minimum criteria using a 5-fold cross-validation to determine the optimal values in the machine learning process.

The study population was divided into train cohort, validation cohort and time test cohort. Using the “glm” R package, we developed a logistic regression (LR) pre­ dictive model in the training cohort incorporating: (1) LASSO-selected genes, (2) overlapping DEGs between cfRNA and placental of FGR, and (3) clinical character­ istics including pre-BMI, maternal age, and gestational age at blood test. The model was subsequently validated in both the validation and time test cohorts. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis was utilized to evaluate the performance of LR model using the “pROC” R package. Calibration curves and decision curve analy­ sis were adopted to evaluate the accuracy of LR model in predicting FGR.

A correlation heatmap was generated using the “cor­ rplot” package in R, based on the study population char­ acteristics and predictive genes. Additionally, box plots of predictive genes expression between the FGR and control groups were created using the “ggboxplot” function from the “ggpubr” package.

Statistical analysis Continuous variables were presented as mean ± stan­ dard deviation and analyzed via Student t test. Categori­ cal variables were shown in proportion and compared by the Chi-square test or Fisher exact test. Statistical differ­ ences in gene expression levels between two groups were assessed via the Wilcoxon test. Pearson correlation analy­ sis was performed to evaluate the associations among study population characteristics and predictive genes.

All statistical analyses were performed using GraphPad Prism 8 and R software (version 4.3). Two-sided P < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.

Results Study population characteristics The flow chart of this study was showed in Fig. 1. A total of 120 pregnant women diagnosed with FGR had NIPT data collected at our hospital. Following exclusion criteria (22 with preeclampsia, 36 with gestational diabetes mel­ litus, 12 twin pregnancies, four with fetal abnormalities, and seven with autoimmune diseases), 39 women with FGR met the inclusion requirements. The 32 FGR sam­ ples were divided into an internal cohort (consisting of training and validation cohorts), with each case matched to approximately four controls, resulting in a total of 127 matched controls. The training cohort (70%) included 24 FGR samples and 87 controls, while the validation cohort (30%) comprised 8 FGR samples and 40 controls. The time test cohort consisted of seven FGR samples and six controls.

The baseline characteristics of the study population were presented in Table 1 and Table S1. Both FGR and control groups underwent blood testing during early to mid-pregnancy, with comparable gestational ages at blood test (15.8 ± 3.9 vs. 14.7 ± 2.9 weeks, P = 0.075) (Fig. S1). The mean gestational age at ultrasound-confirmed FGR diagnosis was significantly later at 32.59 ± 5.0 weeks. We found that gestational age at delivery (P = 0.0008) and birthweight (P < 0.0001) were significantly lower in the FGR group compared to the control group. Additionally, the proportion of neonatal transfer (P = 0.011) was sig­ nificantly higher in FGR group. There were no significant differences between the FGR and control groups in terms of maternal age, pre-BMI, delivery mode, or in vitro fer­ tilization. In the time test cohort, birthweight (P = 0.0013) and pre-BMI (P = 0.004) were significantly lower in the FGR group compared to the control group.

DEGs between FGR and control groups To further identify biomarkers associated with FGR, DEGs analysis was performed on cfRNA expression data from maternal plasma during early and mid-pregnancy, as well as on microarray data from placenta samples, comparing control and FGR groups. A total of 405 DEGs were identified in cfRNA from FGR maternal plasma, including 386 up-regulated genes and 19 down-regulated genes (Fig. 2A and Table S2). In the FGR placenta data­ set, 98 genes were up-regulated and 45 genes were downregulated (Fig. 2B and Table S3). Functional enrichment analysis was performed on the cfRNA DEGs, with the top ten significantly enriched GO terms and KEGG path­ ways presented in Figs. 2C and 3D. The GO enrichment terms included cytoplasmic translation, actin filament

Upon intersect­ ing DEGs from cfRNA and FGR placental data, BIN2 was identified as the hub gene, being up-regulated in both (Fig. 3A).

Identification of predictive genes via machine learning The LASSO regression algorithm was used to screen pre­ dictive genes from cfRNA DEGs. The optimal λ value for the LASSO was chosen through 5-fold cross-validation using the minimum criteria. The coefficients of LASSO versus log (λ) were shown in Fig. 3B and C. A value of λ = 0.139 with log (λ) = -1.972 was chosen. Two predic­ tive genes, OAZ1 and RHOA, were selected for further LR analysis (Table S4). We then analyzed the correlation

between the predictive genes (OAZ1, RHOA and BIN2) and clinical characteristics. The results showed that OAZ1, RHOA and BIN2 were positively correlated with FGR. Additionally, BIN2, RHOA and OAZ1 were posi­ tively correlated with each other (Fig. 3D). In the cfRNA data, RHOA, OAZ1 and BIN2 were up-regulated in FGR group compared to the control group (Fig. 3E).

Development and validation of predictive model In the training cohort, we developed LR models to pre­ dict FGR risk using various combinations of three predictive genes (BIN2, RHOA, OAZ1) and clinical char­ acteristics (pre-BMI, maternal age, and gestational age at blood test). ROC analysis was used to determine the sensitivity, specificity, accuracy and area under the curve (AUC) of the model. Discussion Recently studies have explored the predictive potential of cfRNA in gestation [7, 8]. cfRNA carry information about fetal gene expression and biological processes, persisting in maternal blood for extended periods [14]. In this study, we systematically delineated the cfRNA profiles associ­ ated with FGR in maternal plasma during early and midpregnancy, and integrated placental microarray data to identify hub genes. OAZ1 and RHOA, selected through the LASSO algorithm, were positively associated with FGR. BIN2 was found to be up-regulated in both cfRNA and placenta transcripts in FGR samples compared to controls. A model incorporating BIN2, OAZ1, RHOA, and clinical characteristics (pre-BMI, maternal age, ges­ tational age at blood test) demonstrated high accuracy in predicting the risk of FGR during early to mid-pregnancy. The calibration assessment revealed that the predicted probabilities aligned well with the observed probabilities.

Although there are currently no effective methods for preventing or treating FGR due to its complex etiology [15], it remains crucial in clinical practice to promptly identify high-risk pregnant women and implement

appropriate interventions to reduce the incidence of FGR and prevent adverse pregnancy outcomes. Research­ ers are actively working on developing more accurate, sensitive, and non-invasive methods for diagnosing and screening FGR in early gestation, including the use of bio­ markers, ultrasound technology and metabolic indicators [16–18]. However, Neefjes et al. [19] revealed suboptimal detection rates of FGR through late third-trimester uni­ versal ultrasound screening. Therefore, early identifica­ tion of FGR risk during early to mid-pregnancy, followed by intensified ultrasound surveillance, is essential for timely intervention and improved pregnancy outcomes.

Placental abnormalities are a major cause of FGR, making biochemical markers of placental dysfunction important indicators for identifying the risk of adverse pregnancy outcomes. Previous research on predicting FGR using maternal plasma biomarkers has frequently involved secondary analysis of data from NIPT for fetal aneuploidy. Screening for FGR using maternal factors alone achieved an AUC of 0.719 (95% CI: 0.706–0.732). When combined with additional measurements such as fetal nuchal translucency thickness, pregnancyassociated plasma protein-A and free β-hCG, the AUC increased to 0.747 (95% CI: 0.735–0.760) [20]. Sovio et al. [21] utilized maternal serum metabolite ratio to predict term FGR, achieving an AUC of 0.78 (95% CI: 0.730–0.820). A limitation of using these metabolite ratios is that they rely on relative concentrations rather than absolute units to assess metabolites levels. Soluble fms-like tyrosine kinase-1 and placental growth factor, which reflect the degree of placental insufficiency, have also been used to predict FGR [22, 23]. However, their predictive utility is limited, as these markers are unable to reliably differentiate between FGR associated with preeclampsia and isolated FGR resulting solely from pla­ cental insufficiency [24]. Although both conditions share placental dysfunction as a common pathophysiological feature, they are clinically distinct entities with divergent underlying mechanisms. Importantly, the FGR predic­ tive model developed in our study was constructed inde­ pendently of confounding maternal conditions such as preeclampsia and gestational diabetes mellitus, thereby enhancing its specificity for isolated FGR.

By integrating cfRNA-seq data from maternal plasma and microarray data from FGR placenta, we observed that the hub gene BIN2, which is up-regulated in FGR placenta, could also be detected in maternal plasma dur­ ing early and mid-pregnancy. This finding underscores the potential for detecting placental gene expression from maternal plasma. Further investigation revealed that RHOA, OAZ1 and BIN2 may play important roles in placental development. Phospholipase D is involved in the metabolism and signal transduction of cell membranes, converting phosphatidylcholine into phosphatidic acid and choline. In the human placenta, the activity of phos­ pholipase D plays an important role in maintaining nor­ mal placental function and development.

Recently study revealed that RHOA/ROCK, activated by S1P signaling through GPCR-mediated Gα12/13, primarily regulates cellular cytoskeletal dynamics and medicates trophoblast invasion [27]. Nitric oxide (NO) is essential for the diastolic blood vessels and regulates the implantation of placenta [28]. The RHOA/RHO-kinase pathway negatively regulate NO production in endothe­ lial cells. Rho-kinase inhibitors exhibit potent vasodila­ tory effects and can promote vasodilation, particularly under conditions where vasoconstriction is exacerbated by factors such as increased calcium influx through G-protein-coupled receptor activation, hypoxia, or nitric oxide synthase inhibition. Wang et al. [29] suggested that the level of RHOA promoted neuronal apoptosis and reduced neural stem cells proliferation in FGR.

OAZ1 plays a crucial role in cellular physiological func­ tions. Research has found that the expression of OAZ1 is reduced in certain cancer cells. The loss of OAZ1 expres­ sion can promote the proliferation and metastasis of can­ cer cells, whereas overexpression of OAZ1 can inhibit these processes [30]. BIN2 mediates microtubule move­ ment by interacting with tubulin proteins [31]. However, no relevant studies have yet explored the role of BIN2 in FGR. In our study, GO and KEGG enrichment analyses revealed that the mitogen-activated protein kinase sig­ naling pathway and the metabolism of amino acids and derivatives are associated with embryonic development. Recent studies have demonstrated that the mitogen-acti­ vated protein kinase signaling pathway is a key cellular pathway regulating processes such as cell proliferation, differentiation, and apoptosis [32].

This study presents an easily accessible model for pre­ dicting FGR in early and mid-pregnancy, by combin­ ing non-invasive, readily available cfRNA profiling of maternal plasma with clinical characteristics. Detecting BIN2, OAZ1, and RHOA, which are the genes included in the prediction model, through real-time quantitative polymerase chain reaction (qPCR) is significantly more cost-effective and provides faster results. Despite its con­ tributions, this study has several limitations. It is based on a single-center cohort, which may limit the external validity and generalizability of the findings. Addition­ ally, the relatively small sample size necessitates cau­ tious interpretation of the results. Future multi-center studies with larger cohorts are essential to validate and strengthen these findings.

Conclusions In summary, the prediction model was successfully developed for predicting the risk of FGR based on cfRNA profiling of maternal plasma and clinical characteris­ tics during early and mid-pregnancy. Through compre­ hensive research on the relationship between cfRNA and FGR, we aim to offer clinicians a fast, accurate, and noninvasive tool for FGR prediction. This model could facilitate earlier diagnosis and intervention, potentially improving long-term outcomes.
